title: I've had so many mid life crises
author: Belinda
summary: Belinda uses a failed return to stand up comedy as the frame for an argument about teacher attrition and what schools actually value. The comedy story supplies the diagnosis: she rushed her material and gave nothing time to land, which she notes is the opposite of how she teaches her special education students every day. The pivot comes when she meets an experienced teacher at the same open mic who is burnt out and ready to quit, and her anger turns on a system she describes as breaking teachers and then answering the shortage by recruiting replacements. She reports being in the middle of enterprise bargaining and insists that the media framing around pay misses the point, because the live issues for many teachers are working conditions, the conditions students learn in, and safety. The personal thread and the professional one meet in the idea of value, both learning to value her own varied experience and pressing a system to value teachers, knowledge and expertise. She closes by arguing that the profession argues too much about how and not enough about what, since without clarity on what education, learning and inclusion are, the how cannot be settled.
points: The essay reads teacher burnout from inside the profession, using a chance meeting with a veteran teacher ready to quit as its central evidence rather than statistics.
Belinda charges that the system responds to attrition by recruiting more entrants instead of fixing the conditions driving people out.
She argues that the public bargaining debate is misframed as a pay dispute when the issues keeping teachers awake are conditions and safety.
An employer rejecting a safety claim at the bargaining table is treated as a signal about how much staff are valued, not merely a contractual outcome.
Her closing move is to argue that the sector should settle what education, learning, knowledge and inclusion actually are before litigating the how.
quotes: Last night, I almost spat my material rapid fire at my audience so they didn't even have time for a joke to land let alone be able to laugh before I was onto the next thing. This is especially funny for me because every day I spend with my special education students, I slow things down and give things time to land, to be processed.

At least last night I felt like I had my funny bone back. I'd just lost me. That is the funny thing about stand up, you need to find your voice. I was lucky first time around because I found it straight up. Oh it wasn't all plain sailing then either. Instead of backing myself after a successful open mic night, I tried a stand up comedy course and the teacher broke me. He tried to change my energy and my material, the essence of me really.
The saddest part of the night though was not my performance, unless perhaps you were in the audience. It was meeting a teacher in crisis. This was an experienced teacher, burnt out and ready to quit.

It continually makes me angry that we appear to be working in a system that seems to be breaking teachers, sucking the life out of their well-intentioned bodies and spitting their skins out like they're expendable resources. It makes me even angrier that there doesn't seem to be much happening to fix this. The main focus seems to be on recruiting more fodder.
The cold reality is that at 56 as a serial career changer, I've really got nowhere else to go. I've got to make teaching work. I actually love the kids. It is the system that sucks.

We're in the middle of enterprise bargaining where I am and the focus in the media is all on pay. It's not about pay for many of us - its about conditions. Our conditions. The conditions students are learning in. Our safety. The safety of the school environment your child is meant to be learning in. Pay is nice but for many of us we are experiencing much bigger issues in our schools. It is those frustrations that keep us awake at night.
The system needs to start valuing teachers, knowledge and expertise. When an employer rejects a safety claim in bargaining, they send a strong message about how much they value their employees.

It might be time to stop arguing so much about the details of how and start pushing the narrative to focus on what. If we aren't crystal clear on what education, learning, knowledge and inclusion are, I don't know that we can ever really solve how.
